_note: Thirty second spoken cards, one per destination slug, recorded to media/audio/card-<slug>.mp3 by voice_guides.py --cards. These are the second tier: guide_scripts.json holds the three minute guides for places you travel to and settle into, and this file holds the places you are simply standing in front of. A card runs sixty to a hundred and ten words and voice_guides.py refuses one outside that band at either end, because a card that sprawls has quietly become a bad guide. Same house rules as the long guides: write for the ear, short sentences, one thing worth noticing and one thing to do, numbers spelled out because the reader says digits badly, and no long dashes. /api/destinations finds the recording on disk and offers the button itself, so a new card needs no edit to destinations.json. [SEAN]
ben-s-chili-bowl: Nineteen fifty eight, on U Street, and the half-smoke is the order. It is a half pork half beef sausage, split, grilled, and buried under chili. This building matters beyond the food. During the nineteen sixty eight unrest it was one of the few places allowed to stay open past curfew, feeding police and activists at the same counter. Look at the photographs on the wall on your way in. Cash moves faster than card here at lunch, and the line at one o'clock is worth avoiding.
boston-common-and-public-garden: Sixteen thirty four, which makes this the oldest public park in the country. It was common grazing land first, then a militia field, and the cows only left in eighteen thirty. It runs straight into the Public Garden, and the two are not the same place. The Common is rough and open. The Garden is formal, with the weeping willows and the lagoon. The swan boats have been pedalled by the same family since eighteen seventy seven. They run in warm months only, and the ride is slow on purpose.
carnegie-hall: Eighteen ninety one, and Tchaikovsky himself conducted on the opening night. The acoustics are the reason musicians still care about this room. It was built before amplification and it does not need any. The old joke about how you get to Carnegie Hall, practise, is worn out but the tours are not. They run most afternoons in season and take you into the main hall when it is empty, which is when you can actually hear what the room does. The Rose Museum upstairs is free and takes fifteen minutes.
chelsea-market: This was the Nabisco factory. The Oreo was invented in this building in nineteen twelve, and they left the brick and the pipes exactly where they were. Thirty five vendors now, down one long corridor, tacos and lobster rolls and doughnuts. Notice the waterfall about halfway along, running down an old well shaft they uncovered during the rebuild. Come hungry but come off peak. Between noon and two the corridor stops moving. Buy from two different stalls and eat standing, the way the building was always used.
children-s-museum-of-the-arts: A hands-on art museum for children, where the point is that they make something rather than look at something. Clay, paint, animation, and a ball pit, with studios staffed by working artists. It is aimed at roughly one to fifteen years old, and the younger end is well served, which is rarer than it should be. Sessions and studios run to a timetable, so look at the day's schedule when you arrive and plan around the one your child would care about. Book ahead on weekends and school holidays. Capacity is real and they do fill.
chrysler-building: Nineteen thirty, one thousand and forty six feet, and for eleven months it was the tallest building in the world. It won that title by cheating, beautifully. The architect built the spire in secret inside the shaft, then raised it through the roof in about ninety minutes to beat a rival across town. The eagles at the corners are modelled on the hood ornaments of a nineteen twenty nine Chrysler. There is no observation deck, so the building is something you look at, not from. Do go into the lobby. The red marble and the ceiling mural are free and most people walk past them.
faneuil-hall-marketplace: Three long granite halls of food stalls beside the seventeen forty two meeting house where colonists argued themselves toward revolution. Quincy Market in the middle is the food. The hall itself, the brick building with the grasshopper weather vane on top, is the history, and it is free to walk into. That grasshopper has been up there since seventeen forty two and was once used to test whether a stranger was really from Boston. They would ask what sat on top of Faneuil Hall. Street performers work the plaza between the halls all afternoon.
fenway-park: Nineteen twelve, the oldest ballpark in the major leagues, and the Green Monster still stands thirty seven feet high in left field. The tour runs on non-game days and it puts you inside the Monster, where a hundred years of players have signed the wall in the scoreboard operator's hutch. If you are here for a game, get there early enough to walk Yawkey Way while it fills up. The seats are famously small and some of them face the wrong way, which is what happens when a park is squeezed into city blocks that were already there.
founding-farmers: Owned by a collective of American family farms, which is the whole idea, and it shows up on the plate. Fried chicken and waffles, beignets, and a breakfast taken more seriously than most dinners. The wait can be long because they do not turn tables quickly and they are not trying to. Book ahead. This is not a place to try to walk into at nine on a Saturday. If you are alone, the bar seats are first come and usually open, and the same full menu is served there.
freedom-trail-start: Two and a half miles of red brick line, sixteen sites, starting on Boston Common and ending at Bunker Hill. The line is painted and inlaid into the actual pavement, so you cannot really get lost. You do not have to walk all of it. Most people do the first mile, to Faneuil Hall, and that carries the bulk of the Revolutionary story. Follow the brick rather than a map on your phone. It crosses roads at odd angles on purpose, and looking down keeps you seeing the buildings instead of a screen.
frick-collection: Henry Clay Frick's own house on the Upper East Side, and his pictures are still hung as a collector hung them rather than as a museum would. Vermeer, Rembrandt, Holbein, in rooms with furniture and a garden court, which changes how you look at them. There are only about thirty five Vermeers known in the world and this house has three of them. It is a small museum and that is its advantage. Two hours is plenty. Check the current location and hours before you go, because the collection has been moving between buildings.
georgetown-waterfront: The river at the bottom, the shops of M Street at the top, and Federal row houses in between. Start at the water and walk up, not down, because the hill is gentler that way and the houses reveal themselves as you climb. Look for the old canal a block in from the river. The C and O was cut in the eighteen thirties to carry coal, and the lock gates are still in place. The waterfront park is free, the benches face the Potomac, and sunset over the Key Bridge is the reason to time it.
grand-central-oyster-bar: Downstairs in the belly of the terminal, under Guastavino tile that has been curving overhead since nineteen thirteen. Order at the counter and watch the shuckers work. Before you go in, find the whispering gallery just outside the door. Stand facing one corner of the archway while a friend faces the opposite one, and speak quietly into the tile. They will hear you clearly from thirty feet away. Nobody can explain why it works as well as it does. Then go eat oysters.
greenacre-park: A vest pocket park on East Fifty First Street, about the width of a townhouse, with a twenty five foot waterfall at the back of it. The waterfall is not decoration. It is there to drown out the traffic, and it works completely. Walk in from the street and the city goes quiet in about four steps. It is privately owned and open to the public, which is a New York arrangement worth knowing about. Bring lunch. There are chairs you can move, which sounds small and is the entire design.
harvard-yard-cambridge: Sixteen thirty six, across the river in Cambridge, a green ringed by red brick halls. The John Harvard statue is known as the statue of three lies. It is not John Harvard, he did not found the college, and the date on it is wrong. People rub the shoe for luck. Students will tell you what else happens to that shoe at night, so decide for yourself. Walk out into Harvard Square afterwards for the bookshops. The Yard takes half an hour, and the square is where the neighbourhood actually is.
joe-s-pizza: Nineteen seventy five, and this is the slice every other slice in New York gets measured against. Thin, very hot, folded lengthwise and eaten standing at the shelf by the window. There is no seating worth the name and that is the point. Get the plain cheese first even if you want something else. A plain slice is how you judge a pizzeria, and this one has been passing that test for fifty years. The line moves faster than it looks. Have your money out and know what you want.
katz-s-delicatessen: Eighteen eighty eight, and they still slice the pastrami by hand. You are handed a paper ticket at the door. Do not lose it. That ticket is how you pay, and there is a sign about the fine if it goes missing. Go to the counter, not the table service, and tip the cutter a dollar. He will hand you a warm scrap of pastrami while he works, which is the best bite in the building. One sandwich feeds two people. Order it on rye with mustard and do not ask for mayonnaise.
leslie-lohman-museum-of-art: In SoHo, and it is the first museum in the world dedicated to art about the queer experience, which is the fact worth carrying in with you. It started as two men's private collection in their loft in the nineteen sixties, at a time when showing this work publicly carried real risk, and it became a museum in twenty sixteen. It is small, it is free or pay what you wish, and the shows rotate often. Half an hour is usually right. Check what is currently hanging before you make the trip.
levain-bakery: The cookie weighs six ounces and it is deliberately underbaked in the middle, so the centre is still molten when it reaches you. Chocolate chip walnut is the original. There is almost always a line and it almost always moves. Eat it within about ten minutes. Warm is the entire proposition here, and a Levain cookie an hour later is a good cookie instead of a great one. If the line is long, buy two. You will want the second one and you will not want to queue twice.
mount-rushmore-national-memorial: Four heads, sixty feet each, carved into a granite face in the Black Hills between nineteen twenty seven and nineteen forty one. Most of it was done with dynamite. Ninety percent of the rock came off with explosives placed by men on ropes, and the fine work was finished by hand afterwards. Walk the Presidential Trail below the viewing terrace. It takes about half an hour and it puts you under the chins, which is a completely different sculpture from the postcard angle. Early morning light comes straight onto the faces. By late afternoon they are in shadow.
museum-of-american-history: This is where the actual Star-Spangled Banner is. Not a copy. The flag that was flying over Fort McHenry in eighteen fourteen when Francis Scott Key wrote the words down. It hangs in a dim, cool room at a slight angle, because the fabric can no longer hold its own weight. Give that room ten minutes on its own. People walk through it in ninety seconds and miss it. Lincoln's top hat and the First Ladies' gowns are here too. Entry is free, like every Smithsonian, and you can come back tomorrow for the half you did not see.
museum-of-fine-arts: Half a million works, and it is strongest in three places: the Impressionists, Egyptian art, and American painting. The Egyptian collection is here because the museum ran its own digs at Giza for forty years, so a lot of it came out of the ground with their name on the paperwork. Do not try to see it all. Pick two wings and let the rest go. Wednesday evenings are quieter than weekends, and the light in the Impressionist rooms is better before the afternoon crowd arrives.
museum-of-natural-history-and-planetariu: In Roger Williams Park in Providence, and it is the oldest museum in Rhode Island, opened in eighteen ninety six. Natural history downstairs, planetarium upstairs, and the planetarium is the reason to time your visit. Shows run on a fixed schedule, usually a few a day, and the room is small enough that a busy afternoon sells out. Check the times before you set off. The park around it is worth an hour on its own. There are lakes, a bandstand, and Victorian landscaping that has been there as long as the museum has.
new-england-aquarium: The Giant Ocean Tank runs four storeys up through the middle of the building, and the walkway spirals around it, so you climb through a Caribbean reef rather than looking into it. Sea turtles, sharks and rays, and the turtles are the ones people remember. Start at the top and walk down. Almost everybody goes up first, so going against them means you get the glass to yourself for the first twenty minutes. The harbour seals out front are outdoors and free to watch without a ticket.
old-ebbitt-grill: Washington's oldest saloon, eighteen fifty six, two blocks from the White House. The animal heads over the bar are said to have been shot by Teddy Roosevelt, which the staff will tell you with a straight face and a little doubt. This is a power lunch room. Sit at the oyster bar rather than a table and you will hear more of the city. Happy hour oysters are the value here, and they run late in the evening as well as early. Reserve if you want dinner. Walk in if you want the bar.
paley-park: Three East Fifty Third Street, and it is the pocket park every other pocket park was copied from. Nineteen sixty seven, on the site of the old Stork Club, with honey locust trees, movable chairs and a wall of falling water at the back. The waterfall runs at about the volume of the traffic outside, which is deliberate. It does not silence the city so much as replace it. It is free and it is open to the street on one side only. Sit for ten minutes. That is what it is for.
peter-luger-steak-house: Williamsburg, since eighteen eighty seven, and they have been dry aging their own beef on the premises the whole time. The porterhouse is the order. It arrives already sliced, on a plate tilted so the juices run down, and they will serve it for two, three or four. Bring cash or their own card. They famously do not take most credit cards and people still get caught by that. Ask for the bacon to start. It comes as one thick slab, and it is not a side dish, it is an event.
potomac-water-taxi: The river route between Georgetown, The Wharf and Old Town Alexandria, and it is a genuine shortcut rather than a sightseeing loop. You get the monuments from the water, which is the angle almost nobody photographs, and you skip the traffic that would eat forty minutes on land. Sit outside at the back. The wind is worth it and the wake makes the better picture. Check the last sailing before you commit to a long dinner at the far end, because the timetable thins out in the evening and the road back is slow.
rose-museum: A small free museum inside Carnegie Hall, dedicated to the building itself. Fifteen minutes is enough and it is fifteen minutes well spent before a concert. The story worth knowing is that the hall was nearly demolished in the nineteen sixties. A violinist, Isaac Stern, led the fight to save it, and the main auditorium carries his name now because of that campaign rather than because of his playing. It opens in the afternoon and around performance times, so check before making the trip for it alone.
russian-tea-room: Next door to Carnegie Hall, opened in nineteen twenty seven by dancers from the Russian Imperial Ballet who had left after the revolution and wanted somewhere to drink tea. The interior is deliberately, gloriously too much. Green walls, red banquettes, gold everywhere, and the Christmas decorations stay up all year on purpose. It is expensive for dinner. Tea or a drink at the bar buys you the same room for much less. Book if you want a booth. The tables by the wall are where you want to sit.
st-patrick-s-cathedral: A Gothic cathedral dropped into the middle of Midtown, finished in eighteen seventy eight, when this was still the edge of the built city and people called it a folly. Now the skyscrapers lean over it, which is the whole picture. It is free and it is open, and services run through the day. Step inside even for five minutes. The temperature drops and the traffic noise stops at the door, which is the point of the building. Look up at the rose window over the Fifth Avenue entrance from the inside, not the outside.
statue-of-liberty-ferry: The ferry leaves from Battery Park and it is the only way to stand under her. Ellis Island is the second stop, and it is the one people are surprised by. Forty percent of Americans have somebody in that building's records. Watch for the moment the boat clears the seawall and the whole harbour opens at once. Everyone rushes the right rail. Go left instead, toward Brooklyn, and you get the skyline with nobody's elbow in it. Book the timed ticket before you come, because the security line at the dock is the real wait, not the boat.
stone-street: One of the oldest paved streets in Manhattan, and the cobbles are real. It was the Dutch who paved it, in the sixteen fifties, because the cart traffic kept churning the mud. Now it is a single narrow lane of pubs with tables down the middle. In warm months the whole street becomes one long outdoor room and the buildings block the wind. Come after five on a weekday and you are drinking with the financial district. Come at noon on a Sunday and you have the street almost to yourself.
the-morgan-library: J. P. Morgan's private library, built in nineteen oh six to hold one man's collection, and the original room is the reason to come. Three storeys of walnut bookcases, a painted ceiling, and a vault door in the corner. There are three Gutenberg Bibles in this building. Most institutions in the world have none. The modern galleries alongside show manuscripts and drawings in rotation, so what is out changes. Go into the old study next to the library, the red room. Morgan did his actual business in there, and it looks it.
the-renee-and-chaim-gross-foundation: The sculptor Chaim Gross lived and worked in this Greenwich Village house, and the foundation kept it as it was rather than turning it into a gallery. His studio is on the ground floor with the tools where he left them, and the family's own art collection is upstairs in the rooms they lived in. Visits are by appointment and in small groups, so this is a plan-ahead place, not a walk-in. That is also why it is good. You are in somebody's house, not a museum, and it is very quiet.
the-wharf: A mile of restaurants and music halls along the Potomac, built beside the Municipal Fish Market. That market has been trading on this water since eighteen five, which makes it the oldest continuously operating fish market in the country, older than Fulton in New York. Go to the market end first, before the restaurants. Buy crab from a barge, eat it standing at the rail, and then walk the boardwalk. In the evening there is usually live music spilling out of at least one door, free to stand and listen to.
union-market: Forty plus vendors under one bright roof in Northeast, dumplings and Korean tacos and local oysters. This was a wholesale market district for a century, and the neighbourhood around it is still half warehouse, half new construction, which is worth a look in itself. Come with more than one appetite and split everything. The stalls are small on purpose so you can eat across four of them. Weekday afternoons are calm and the vendors will talk to you. Saturday is a crowd.
united-nations-headquarters: The land is in Manhattan but it is not United States territory. It is international ground, with its own post office and its own stamps, which you can only post from here. The guided tour is the only way past the lobby, it is booked in advance, and you need photo identification. Look for the sculpture of the revolver with its barrel tied in a knot, near the visitors' entrance. Tours do not run when the General Assembly is in session in the autumn, so check the calendar first.
us-capitol-visitor-center: Tours start underground, which surprises people, and come up into the Crypt beneath the Rotunda. Book the free tour in advance online. Walk-up slots exist but they run out early. In Statuary Hall, ask your guide to show you the listening spot. Each state sent two statues, and the room's curved ceiling carries a whisper from one side clean across to the other. John Quincy Adams is said to have used it to hear the opposition talking. Your bag will be screened, so travel light and leave food and liquids behind.
uss-constitution: Old Ironsides, launched seventeen ninety seven, and still a commissioned ship in the United States Navy, which makes her the oldest warship afloat anywhere in the world. Active duty sailors give the tours, in uniform, and they are the reason to come. The nickname is literal. In the war of eighteen twelve, British shot was seen bouncing off her hull, because it is live oak twenty five inches thick in places. Bring photo identification. She sits on an active naval base and you go through a security check to reach her.
waldorf-astoria-hotel: The hotel that gave the world room service and the Waldorf salad, and moved here in nineteen thirty one when the Empire State Building took its original site. There is a private railway platform underneath it, track sixty one, built so that guests could arrive without being seen. Franklin Roosevelt is said to have used it. It has been through a long closure and restoration, so check whether the public rooms are open before you plan around it. Even from the pavement, the Art Deco doors on Park Avenue are worth the two minutes.
white-house-lafayette-sq: Lafayette Square gives you the classic north face, the one on the twenty dollar bill. This is as close as most visitors get, and it is close enough for the photograph. An actual tour has to be requested through your member of Congress, and the lead time is weeks, sometimes months, so it is not a thing you decide to do today. Look at the square itself while you are here. It has been the country's front lawn for protest since the eighteen hundreds, and there is almost always somebody making a point on it.
